sub_agendas_items.title: July 1 Extreme Weather Event Update

motions.motion_text: That the Rules of Procedure be suspended to consider the following motions to provide timely direction in response to the July 1 Extreme Weather Event.

WHEREAS on July 1, 2026, the City of Ottawa experienced a historic rainfall event; and
WHEREAS staff have received as of July 14, 2026, approximately 6000 service requests from residents whose homes experienced basement flooding as a result of this storm event; and
WHEREAS the City of Ottawa offers two programs to assist residential property owners affected by flooding: the Compassionate Grant Program and the Residential Protective Plumbing Program; and
WHEREAS the City of Ottawa's Residential Protective Plumbing Program provides financial assistance to qualified City of Ottawa property owners for the installation of protective plumbing devices such as sump pumps and storm and sanitary backwater valves; and
WHEREAS the City of Ottawa's Compassionate Grant Program provides financial assistance to qualified City of Ottawa property owners and tenants affected by flooding due to a sewer surcharge event; and
WHEREAS eligibility for the Compassionate Grant program is as follows:
WHEREAS staff have observed an increase in applications to both the Residential Protective Plumbing Program and the Compassionate Grant Program following the July 1, 2026, storm, which may result in funding requirements exceeding currently available resources; and
WHEREAS all applications submitted under the Compassionate Grant Program will require staff verification to confirm that the property experienced flooding as a result of the July 1, 2026, storm event;
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT Council waive the eligibility requirement that applicants must not have received a Compassionate Grant within the previous five years, and the requirement that the flooding be attributable to a sewer surcharge event, for claims arising from the July 1, 2026, storm event; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Council delegate authority to the General Manager of Infrastructure and Water Services to grant exceptions to the Compassionate Grant Program eligibility requirements, where deemed appropriate, for applications arising from the July 1, 2026, storm event; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT if applications for financial assistance exceed the current capital funding budgets ofthe Residential Protective Plumbing Program and the Compassionate Grant Program, that staff report back to Committee and Council on the financial implications as part of the 2027 Capital Adjustments and Closing of Projects – City Tax and Rate Supported report; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT the City’s Public Information and Media Relations unit (PIMR) establish and launch a promotional awareness campaign to ensure all flood-impacted residents, as well as residents citywide, learn about this program, its benefits, and how they can apply.

WHEREAS on July 1, 2026 an extreme weather event impacted the City of Ottawa, which caused extensive flooding and damage to almost 6,000 homes and properties across the city; and
WHEREAS it is appropriate that direction be provided as soon as possible to City of Ottawa staff to assist in the storm recovery process;
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the Rules of Procedure be suspended to permit the introduction of the following motion:
WHEREAS on July 1, 2026, an extreme weather event impacted the city of Ottawa causing extensive flooding as well as damage to trees and property; and
WHEREAS repair or renovations of affected homes and buildings will be required and property owners may have to obtain demolition and/or building permits in order to repair existing buildings and structures in the areas affected by the flooding; and
WHEREAS the cost of these permits would cause additional hardship to the impacted residents, who are already reeling from the financial toll of these floods;
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that Council delegate the authority to the General Manager, Planning, Development and Building Services to suspend the following fees that may be incurred as a direct result of damage inflicted by the extreme weather event of July 1, 2026:

WHEREAS residents continue to cope with the significant emotional, physical, and financial impacts of flooding to their homes arising from the July 1, 2026 flood event; and
WHEREAS some residents who have insurance have been further distressed to learn that they may not be eligible for insurance coverage for some or all of their damages; and
WHEREAS the City is not in a position to provide legal advice to residents, but recognizing timely access to legal information, guidance and assistance is important for residents affected by the floods, including seniors, vulnerable individuals, and those living on fixed or limited incomes; and
WHEREAS community legal clinics and community information sessions can play an important role in helping residents access information and resources regarding insurance coverage issues;
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT the City Solicitor, on behalf of Council, be directed to engage members of Ottawa legal’s community, including through organizations such as the County of Carleton Law Association and Pro Bono Ontario to request that legal professionals with expertise in insurance coverage support affected residents by assisting community legal clinics and participating in any future public information sessions, with the goal of improving residents’ access to timely legal information, guidance, and independent legal advice respecting insurance coverage disputes, claims processes, and related recovery challenges arising from the flooding event; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT City staff facilitate the logistics and promotion of these information sessions so they are broadly advertised and attended by all impacted residents who require this legal information and guidance.

WHEREAS the Canadian Red Cross is a leading organization in helping communities respond to natural disasters across Canada, having helped over a million Canadians recover following disasters and weather events over the last 10 years; and
WHEREAS thousands of Ottawa residents continue to cope with the significant emotional, physical, and financial impacts of flooding to their homes arising from the July 1, 2026 extreme weather and flood event; and
WHEREAS recovering from these floods will take residents many months, and will require a variety of services, including individual needs and social services, guidance on insurance claim matters, referrals for repair and rebuild, and expertise in engineering and renovations to help inform difficult decisions as they rebuild; and
WHEREAS the Canadian Red Cross offers those services as part of a suite of case management and navigational support services it provides to municipalities as they help their residents recover from these events;
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that City Council endorse this partnership between the City of Ottawa and the Canadian Red Crossenabling the Red Cross to serve as the lead non-governmental organization; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that City staff work with the Red Cross to augment the City’s recovery, ensuring they are deployed to all impacted neighbourhoods as soon as possible, with priority given to vulnerable residents, and that their presence and outreach to our residents be facilitated by City staff; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that City staff work with the Red Cross to establish a mechanism to provide the most up-to-date information to impacted councillors regarding the progress of their outreach, assessment, case management and navigational support to affected residents; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that City staff review the impact of this partnership to the event’s response as part of their post-response review, and that they report back to Council no later than Q1 2027; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the City Manager work with the Canadian Red Cross to execute an agreement for this suite of services, at a cost of no more than $400,000 for the period of up to six months of service offering, as is customary under this program; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVEDthat the funding for this initiative be funded through the Tax Stabilization Reserve, with the allocation to be confirmed through the annual disposition report; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that City staff explore a longer-term partnership with the Canadian Red Cross, including on how we can make our community, its infrastructure and the homes of our residents more resilient and better prepared for future extreme weather events, which are now more and more common.

WHEREAS the July 1, 2026, extreme rainfall event caused significant flooding impacts across the City of Ottawa; and
WHEREAS preliminary City data as of July 10 shows that the highest rainfall totals recorded through rain gauges were in the west end, including 167 millimetres at Britannia, 151 millimetres at Colonnade, and 144 millimetres at Nepean; and
WHEREAS preliminary City data as of July 10 indicates that Wards 7, 8 and 9 accounted for approximately 83 percent of flood-related service requests city-wide; and
WHEREAS the City is undertaking a city-wide review of the July 1, 2026, event, including analysis of service requests, previous studies, infrastructure performance and opportunities to improve flood resilience; and
WHEREAS several communities within Ward 9 experienced significant flooding during both the August 10, 2023, and July 1, 2026, extreme rainfall events, suggesting the need to better understand recurring flooding patterns and localized vulnerabilities; and
WHEREAS following the August 10, 2023, event, the City undertook several flood investigations and engineering studies, which identified various flooding mechanisms, infrastructure constraints and drainage challenges; and
WHEREAS residents, community organizations and previous City-led investigations have raised concerns regarding a range of factors that may contribute to flood risk, including infrastructure performance, drainage patterns, overland flow, redevelopment, intensification, site alteration, grading changes and increasing impervious surfaces; and
WHEREAS Graham Creek is a major drainage corridor serving a large watershed that passes through several communities in Wards 7, 8 and 9 highly impacted by the July 1 event, and previous studies have identified increased runoff volumes, more intense rainfall and debris accumulation as important risks to the system; and
WHEREAS the May 2017 Graham Creek Stormwater Infrastructure Public Infrastructure Engineering Vulnerability Committee (PIEVC) Study identified climate-related vulnerabilities within the Graham Creek system while also recommending that future planning be informed by updated climate information, continued analysis, and considerations for system improvements, as new information becomes available; and
WHEREAS the City completed the Graham Creek Storm Infrastructure Renewal Project in 2022 as a climate-resilience initiative, and the project subsequently received the Ontario Public Works Association Public Works Project of the Year Award for Environmental Sustainability – Climate Resilient Infrastructure; and
WHEREAS Graham Creek has been identified as one of seven Priority 1 areas that are recommended to have stormwater retrofit studies completed as part the Stormwater Retrofit Master Plan (Section 10.3 of the Infrastructure Master Plan); and
WHEREAS the July 1, 2026, rainfall event provides an important opportunity to compare observed conditions against previous studies, modelling assumptions, infrastructure investments and climate-resilience planning efforts;
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT Council direct staff, as part of the City's broader review of the July 1, 2026 extreme rainfall event, to examine the factors that contributed to the impacts experienced in Wards 7, 8, 9, and other hard hit wards, including infrastructure performance, drainage systems, watershed conditions, development patterns, stormwater management practices, maintenance considerations and climate-related factors, and report back with findings and recommendations; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT staff compare the July 1, 2026, event with previous flooding events, investigations and studies, including the August 10, 2023, flooding event, to identify recurring flood locations, recurring vulnerabilities and emerging risks; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT staff assess the performance of major watersheds, drainage systems and flood-mitigation infrastructure within affected areas, including Graham Creek, and identify opportunities to incorporate or accelerate stormwater retrofit, stream rehabilitation, conveyance, attenuation, retention, storage and other retrofit measures where appropriate; and also to compare observed conditions with previous modelling, assumptions and design expectations where appropriate; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT staff review whether current planning, drainage review, stormwater management and site alteration processes remain appropriate to identify and mitigate flood risks associated with redevelopment, intensification and changing drainage conditions in established neighbourhoods; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT staff identify opportunities to improve flood resilience through operational, planning, policy, infrastructure, watershed management and climate adaptation measures, including both localized and watershed-scale solutions; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT staff report back as soon as practicable with recommended short-, medium- and long-term actions, including any required future studies, infrastructure priorities, policy considerations, inter-agency coordination opportunities and budget implications.

WHEREAS the storm on July 1 devastated thousands of homes in the City of Ottawa by flooding, with an intensity and volume of water not before seen in the City of Ottawa; and,
WHEREAS the flooding experienced was due to a combination of factors including overland flooding, sanitary and storm sewer surcharges, and others; and
WHEREAS Infrastructure and Water Services has committed to a comprehensive review of this extreme weather event to ‘better understand impacts, assess system performance, and identify areas for improvement’ (Memo sent July 11, 2026 to Council); and ,
WHEREAS College Ward has received the greatest number of flood related service requests across the city, with 2,282 requests, followed by Bay Ward with 1,512 requests and Knoxdale-Merivale with 684 requests; and
WHEREAS affected residents are concerned about specific variables in their neighbourhoods that could have compounded or exacerbated the flooding experienced in their homes, including ditch maintenance and rehabilitation, aging stormwater infrastructure, increased infill development, major construction projects, and parkland saturation.
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the review by Infrastructure and Water Services assess and report back on the following, with a particular focus on the areas of the city most impacted by the extreme weather event on July 1st, namely, but not limited to, Wards 7, 8, and 9:
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that assessment results be released through a phased rollout, where practicable, as information becomes available with communication to neighbourhoods as their assessments are completed.

DIRECTION TO STAFF (Councillor L. Dudas)
Severe weather events are becoming more frequent and can generate significant demand on 3-1-1 services within a short period of time. During major storms, many resident reports involve important but non-life-threatening issues that require timely logging, assessment, and response by the City.
Recent events, such as the July 1, 2026 storm, demonstrated that high call volumes limit residents' ability to report both urgent concerns, such as severe flooding, and other less urgent, though still important issues, such as fallen trees blocking sidewalks, pathways, or park spaces. Providing residents with effective online reporting options for storm-related service requests would help improve access to City services while reducing pressure on 3-1-1 operations during emergency events.
That staff be directed to review opportunities to enhance the City's use of online service requests and digital communications during emergency events in order to support emergency response efforts, improve the client experience, and reduce pressure on 3-1-1 operations, including:
As part of this review, staff report on existing and planned initiatives that are improving the customer experience and reducing demand on 3-1-1 services, including the use of confirmation pages, emails, and other digital communications to provide residents with clear information on next steps, service expectations, and emergency-related updates.

sub_agendas_items.minutes:
DIRECTION TO STAFF (Councillor M. Luloff)
That Council direct staff to report back to the appropriate Standing Committee no later than the end of 2029 on the implementation and effectiveness of the Rental Renovation Licence By-law, including the number of applications received, licences issued, instances of non-compliance, warnings and charges, repeat applications involving the same properties or landlords, operating costs, privacy impacts, interaction with the strengthened provincial framework, and any evidence that the by-law has reduced unlawful renovation-related evictions.
DIRECTION TO STAFF (Councillor S.Plante)
That, as part of the implementation of the Rental Renovation Licence By-law, staff include a link to the existing Landlord and Tenant Rental Housing Property Management By-law Education Guides developed in 2021 in the Eviction Education Guide to be developed as part of the Rental Renovation Licence By-law so that tenants have easy access to tailored, accessible communications and education resources for renters regarding their rights and the municipal tools available to support safe and well-maintained rental housing, recognizing Ottawa’s longstanding and robust rental population, including students, military and diplomatic personnel, and a highly mobile workforce, as well as the anticipated growth in renter households from approximately 36 percent of households today to 43 percent over the next decade; and
That staff include references and links to the existing Landlord and Tenant Rental Housing Property Management Education Guides in their communications to the public and interest holders regarding the Rental Renovation Licence By-law and Eviction Education Guide to help ensure that tenants and landlords are aware of their ongoing rights and responsibilities with respect to the maintenance of rental properties;
That staff be directed to consider, for inclusion as part of the next Term of Council By-law Review Workplan, a review of regulatory options to promote safe and well-maintained rental housing, informed by lessons learned through the Problematic Properties Pilot in Wards 12 and 14 and the implementation of the Rental Renovation Licence By-law, including consideration of a broader apartment building standards and licensing regime and tools such as a Residents First (City of Cleveland) program, a public-facing building rating system similar to the City of Toronto’s RentSafeTO program, and how information from the Problematic Properties Pilot and the Rental Renovation Licence By-law can be used to support the early identification of landlords or properties that may present an elevated risk of non-compliance, as well as proactive inspections and enhanced compliance and enforcement tools to address persistently problematic properties and landlords; and
That staff explore opportunities to share relevant data and compliance information collected through the Problematic Properties Pilot with the staff responsible for administering the Rental Renovation Licence By-law.

sub_agendas_items.title: Joint Aquatic Sports Centre – MOU with Carleton University

motions.motion_text:
WHEREAS the City of Ottawa is experiencing sustained population growth and increasing demand for aquatic facilities, with current capacity insufficient to meet community needs, competitive sport requirements, and public programming demand; and
WHEREAS the Parks and Recreation Facility Master Plan identifies the need for a new 50 metre aquatic facility to address both current deficiencies and future growth pressures; and
WHEREAS a 50-metre aquatic facility would increase Ottawa Tourism’s ability to attract and host provincial, national and international sporting events; and
WHEREAS Carleton University has demonstrated readiness to partner with the City through a significant financial contribution, provision of serviced land, and the ability to advance construction within an accelerated timeline; and
WHEREAS in July 2024, Council approved non-binding confidential negotiations that have led to mutually agreed upon high level principles for the framework of a future agreement; and
WHEREAS the proposed Joint Aquatic Sports Centre would represent a major city building investment supporting community recreation, high performance sport, economic development, and sport tourism; and
WHEREAS the development of a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) is required to formalize shared principles, roles, and governance, and to enable the project to proceed with a more refined design and financial model, value engineering, and updated cost estimates; and
WHEREAS establishing a formal partnership framework through an MOU is necessary to demonstrate project readiness and alignment, which is a prerequisite for pursuing external funding opportunities, including federal and provincial infrastructure programs; and
WHEREAS the Government of Canada has identified community recreation infrastructure as a funding priority, including through programs such as the Build Communities Strong Fund, for which this project may be eligible; and
WHEREAS advancing design and entering into the MOU will reduce financial, technical, and partnership risks by improving cost certainty, refining scope, and clarifying long term responsibilities prior to any final commitment; and
WHEREAS the MOU is expressly non binding and preserves full Council authority over any future capital funding decisions, binding agreements, or construction approvals;
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that Council delegate authority to the General Manager, Recreation, Cultural and Facility Services to finalize and execute an MOU with Carleton University for the development of a Joint Aquatic Sports Centre, to the satisfaction of the City Solicitor; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Council direct staff to utilize the MOU framework to advance discussions with Carleton University and undertake the technical and financial due diligence required to:
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that any agreement enhance public access and time availability of the facility for local residents; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Council direct staff to actively pursue federal and provincial funding opportunities as well as sponsorship and naming rights opportunities, to offset capital costs and minimize the City’s financial exposure; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Council confirms that execution of the MOU does not commit the City to construction, final capital funding, or binding agreements, and that all such decisions will be subject to future Council approval.

I ❤︎ (Heart) Barrhaven Market, Autumn 2026

motions.motion_text:
WHEREAS the I ❤︎ (Heart) Barrhaven Market is a semi-annual event organised by the Ottawa Farmers’ Market in partnership with Locally Crafted Markets and the Barrhaven Business Improvement Area (BIA), promoting the usual local farmers plus guest artisan and business vendors; and
WHEREAS the autumn 2026 market is scheduled for Sunday 20 September 2026 from 10:00 am to 2:00 pm at the Nepean Woods Park and Ride; and
WHEREAS vendors require two hours before and after the market for set up and tear down; and
WHEREAS the market has steadily grown in popularity, becoming one of Barrhaven’s central and most-looked-forward-to regular events and increasing pressure on parking availability at the park and ride; and
WHEREAS potential additional guest vendor space was identified on the bus-only ramp connecting eastbound buses from Nepean Woods Station with eastbound Strandherd Drive, adjacent to the parking lot; and
WHEREAS within the proposed closure timeframe, trips on routes 70, 74, and 99 will need to be placed on a minor detour which adds 60 to 90 seconds to trip time, with no impact to bus stops, no modifications to stop assignments at Nepean Woods Station, and no impact to the turnaround loop for route 80; and
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that Council approve the closure of the bus-only ramp from Nepean Woods Station to Strandherd Drive on Sunday 20 September 2026 from 8:00 am to 4:00 pm for the I ❤︎ (Heart) Barrhaven Market, and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the cost of pylons to demarcate the closed areas and an accessible temporary curb ramp be covered by the event organisers.

sub_agendas_items.title: Preserving of the Kanata golf lands and greenspace
sub_agendas_items.description: Note: The Curry/Sutcliffe Motion of which Notice was previously given at the June 24, 2026, City Council meeting was replaced with the following revised motion pursuant to Subsection 59(5) of the Procedure By-law.

motions.motion_text:
WHEREAS the lands municipally known as 7000 Campeau Drive – formerly the Kanata Lakes Golf and Country Club, and referred to throughout this motion as the Kanata golf lands and greenspace – comprise approximately 175 acres within the Kanata Lakes community, and were made subject to a 1981 agreement known as the 40% Agreement, requiring that 40 per cent of the area be preserved as open space; and
WHEREAS when the urban boundary was extended to allow this area to be developed, the community was promised a Central Park – one large, connected network of greenspace for the whole community; and
WHEREAS the community was allowed, under the Agreement, to use these lands as a winter park, and has done so for more than 40 years, a winter park it has now lost on top of never receiving the Central Park it was promised; and
WHEREAS the roads, water infrastructure, and school capacities in the area, along with the thousands of nearby new apartment units were all planned on the understanding that this land would remain parkland and storm water management for the area; and
WHEREAS hundreds of acres of nearby forests and greenspace were approved for housing development on the understanding that the Kanata golf lands would become the community’s permanent and protected park and greenspace; and
WHEREAS Council has already affirmed, on January 28, 2026, that building homes or other development on these lands does not fit with the plan the broader Kanata Lakes community was built around or the promises made to its residents, and the City has gone through the courts and exhausted its options to enforce the 40% Agreement meant to protect these lands; and
WHEREAS the Ontario Land Tribunal has approved a draft plan of subdivision and municipal zoning for development on these lands, establishing a precedent that long-standing commitments to preserve parkland and greenspace can be overridden through litigation, a precedent every Ontario municipality should want to avoid; and
WHEREAS the Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO) has written to the Attorney General of Ontario asking the Province to review the ClubLink decisions in Ottawa and ensure municipalities have the tools they need to protect open space; and
WHEREAS the Province has stepped in before in similar circumstances – intervening in 2021, after the Town of Oakville passed similar resolutions, to preserve the Glen Abbey Golf Course;
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the Mayor write to the Premier of Ontario and the Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing requesting that the Province of Ontario consider using the following tools:

motions.motion_text:
That the Rules of Procedure be suspended to consider the following motion due to transfer of ownership of 1316 Dorchester Avenue and the preference to resolve the encroachment matter expeditiously.
WHEREAS the original house located at 1316 Dorchester was torn down and a modern home was built this decade which added a secondary dwelling unit and included approximately $100,000 in development charges and other fees to the City of Ottawa; and
WHEREAS 1316 Dorchester Avenue was recently sold and transferred to a new owner (current owner); and
WHEREAS the previous owner has become aware of an issue with regards to the encroachment of stairs onto City of Ottawa property; and
WHEREAS the previous owner has committed to taking steps to legalize the location of the stairs via a survey and legal agreement with the City of Ottawa; and
WHEREAS while the legal agreement would resolve the issue at hand, the encroachment of the stairs would necessitate an annual encroachment fee of approximately $30; and
WHEREAS the encroachment of the stairs occurred at no fault of the current owner and they were not aware of this issue at the time of purchase.
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the requirement of an annual encroachment fee relating to the stairs at 1316 Dorchester Avenue be permanently waived.

sub_agendas_items.title: Halloween Haunted House

motions.motion_text:
WHEREAS the City received a complaint regarding a residence on Pintail Terrace in Orléans, who transformed their property into a popular annual Halloween haunted house attraction; and
WHEREAS  the City requires adequate time to work with the homeowner to ensure compliance;
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the Rules of Procedure be suspended to permit the introduction of the following motion:
WHEREAS the Albert family, residing on Pintail Terrace in Orléans, has transformed their property into a popular annual Halloween haunted house attraction for the past 26 years; and
WHEREAS this seasonal community presentation has operated continuously as an official fundraiser for the CHEO Foundation, successfully raising more than $100,000 to support eastern Ontario’s children’s hospital; and
WHEREAS the event relies heavily on local high school student volunteers earning community service hours and fosters deep community involvement; and
WHEREAS the display includes a decorative castle facade and enclosed walkway spanning portions of the driveway and side yard; and
WHEREAS following a recent complaint, Ottawa By-law and Regulatory Services found elements of this longstanding display does not strictly align with the provisions of City of Ottawa Zoning By-law concerning accessory structures on residential properties; and
WHEREAS a public petition to preserve the tradition has rapidly gathered over 3,000 signatures from Ottawa residents, demonstrating overwhelming community support and showcasing a shared civic desire to keep the display active;
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT staff from By-law and Regulatory Services and Building Code Services be requested to work with the property owner to review available regulatory and planning options, that may permit the continued operation of the charitable Halloween display while ensuring compliance with applicable by-laws and regulations.

motions.motion_text:

WHEREAS on June 24, 2026 Council passed a repeal and replacement of By-law 2002-189, with respect to the licensing and regulation of businesses (the Licensing By-law);and
WHEREAS as part of the updated Licensing By-law a one-day or less license option for refreshment vendors at special events at a lower cost than the current license options was established to come into effect as of January 2027; and
WHEREAS a large number of special events occur during the summer and fall; and
WHEREAS Council wishes to support a diverse economy and vibrant, livable communities; and
WHEREAS on June 24, 2026 Council passed a motion to reduce the license fee payable by refreshment vendors and itinerant sellers for a one-day special event at a cost of $100, from July 15, 2026 to December 31, 2026 in order to maximize the cost savings for refreshment vendor businesses during their most active season.
WHEREAS the fee reduction to $100, from July 15, 2026 to December 31, 2026, as outlined in the motion did not indicate that the processing fee for the license would be included;

WHEREAS the One Million Canadian Hearts initiative, which is empowering Canadians with heart health knowledge and enabling swift interventions that save lives, is building a prevention model that could change how health care is delivered.

sub_agendas_items.title: OCC-2026-15 - Support for tenants in multi-residential buildings during extreme weather events
sub_agendas_items.minutes:
Submitted by T. Kavanagh
On July 1st, the City of Ottawa experienced an unprecedented extreme weather event, with 1000s of residents still dealing with recovery and clean up.
The severity of the storm led to storm led to widespread flooding and significant property damage, resulting in 5,423 service requests related to flooding and weather impacts (as of July 10, 2026), with the most impacted neighbourhoods in Wards 7,8,9, and 4. The storm was particularly devastating for residents at 30 McEwen, a 24 storey, 228 unit building in Bay Ward. The storm resulted in flooding, and catastrophic damage to the building’s electrical system, resulting in a long-term power outage. While residents were strongly encouraged to evacuate, there was no mandatory evacuation order, and for some tenants, no viable place to stay. Many had just paid their month’s rent on July 1st, so were left without enough funds to easily pay for a hotel or other accommodation. While this situation was unique, many tenants across Ottawa found themselves in similar situations following the storm. Given that the City needs to prepare for more frequent extreme weather events, there is a need for more information on supports for tenants in privately owned multi-residential buildings.

sub_agendas_items.title: OCC-2026-16 - July 1 Severe Weather Event
sub_agendas_items.minutes:
Submitted by Councillor L. Johnson
On July 1, the City of Ottawa experienced a severe weather event that impacted and continues to impact thousands of residents with 2500 homes flooded in college ward.
The General Manager of Emergency and Protective Services has stated that the City was ready on July 1st for an emergency as it was already in Enhanced Operations on Canada Day. But it became clear quickly that the required response was more significant than Enhanced Operations, and the full Emergency Command Centre was required.

sub_agendas_items.title: OCC-2026-17 - Cellular Service Coverage and Reliability in City Telecommunications Contracts
sub_agendas_items.minutes:
Submitted by Councillor S. Desroches
Reliable cellular service is no longer a convenience—it is a critical public safety and operational requirement. Every day, City employees rely on mobile communications to deliver essential services, coordinate field operations, and respond to emergencies. During power outages, severe weather events, or other emergencies, dependable cellular service becomes even more critical to maintaining business continuity, supporting emergency response, and communicating with residents.
As Ottawa continues to grow, particularly in communities such as Riverside South and Findlay Creek, every City employee should be able to count on reliable cellular service, regardless of where they are working. The City's telecommunications contracts should reflect a simple principle: "No service, no City contract." If a provider cannot deliver dependable service where the City operates, it should not be entrusted with the City's telecommunications business.

sub_agendas_items.title: OCC-2026-18 - Habitat for Humanity
sub_agendas_items.minutes:
Submitted by Councillor M. Carr
Considerable progress has been made this term of Council on incentives for affordable rental housing as well as incentives for housing in the private market, targeted at both the rental and ownership markets.
Discussions and actions around affordable home ownership, however, have not been a focus with only 35 units underway this term of council. The city has worked with Habitat for Humanity to complete two units in Orleans and recently there was a groundbreaking ceremony for 33 units on Beechcliffe in Ward 9. These units, which are being built by Habitat in partnership with Caivan, included investment in funding and land from the city, and investment of additional funding from the province.
The desire for affordable home ownership for these 33 units was so strong that after 1200 applicants applied for 33 homes in just 5 days, Habitat for Humanity had to shut down the application page. 25 homeowners have already been chosen, with some participating in last week’s groundbreaking. These homeowners are permanently removed from housing precarity and require no more public support for housing.
Habitat is the only non profit that delivers affordable home ownership in the Greater Ottawa area, but yet there is little work being done to promote and support affordable home ownership in Ottawa. Habitat exclusively builds affordable family size housing of 3+ bedrooms, which are units that are in large demand in Ottawa. Families with children under age 18 are given priority. Habitat works with hard working low to moderate income people in the Ottawa and surrounding area, with people with a household income of as low as 70k. They have served numerous applicants who are currently in Ottawa Community Housing and have served applicants who were at risk of becoming homeless. Some Habitat Homeowner applicants are reporting present day rents that are higher than what their future mortgage payment under Habitat home ownership will be.
In light of this need that is being filled by Habitat, could staff please indicate:
Which area of the City is responsible for furthering work on affordable home ownership?
How could the City work with Habitat to establish a pipeline of projects and funding commitments over the long term? This could include a pipeline of land so that mid to long term planning could occur and the organization could fundraise well in advance of shovels being in the ground?
How could the City facilitate the development of left over land from private developments to Habitat and/or support partnerships with private developers to work with Habitat to deliver some level of affordability to all new developments?
How could the City facilitate the collaboration of non profit housing developers to work together on donated land that includes home ownership (Build Now project in Kitchener Waterloo)
How could a portion of funding from the affordable housing capital budget be reserved for affordable home ownership?
